Series::cauchy_¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series& Series::cauchy_() const
Series& Series::cauchy_(double median) const
Series& Series::cauchy_(double median, double sigma) const

What It Does¶

Overwrites every element of the receiver with an independent draw from a Cauchy distribution — a symmetric, bell-ish curve with much heavier tails than a normal. Defaults are median = 0 and sigma = 1.

median is the center (the distribution is symmetric about it); sigma is the half-width at half-maximum — larger sigma spreads the central mass wider. Internally each sample is median + sigma * tan(pi * (U - 0.5)) for a uniform U — a transformed uniform_ fill.

The defining feature: a Cauchy distribution has no finite mean and no finite variance. A running sample average does not settle down as you draw more values — it keeps jumping whenever a large tail sample appears. Use the median and quantiles, never the arithmetic mean, to summarize Cauchy samples. It is a poor model choice anywhere downstream logic assumes a finite variance.

Like the other in-place samplers, the receiver supplies the shape, dtype, platform, and storage; its current values are discarded.

Reproducibility¶

Deterministic given the process-wide RNG seed. Call pluss::rng_seed(seed) before sampling to fix the values; two runs from the same seed produce equal tensors. Each call advances a stream counter.

Parameters¶

median (double, default 0): the center of symmetry. Must be finite.

sigma (double, default 1): the scale (half-width at half-maximum). Must be finite and > 0.

Returns¶

Series& A reference to the receiver, now holding the samples. The write is in-place and preserves storage identity — every alias sees the values.

Raises¶

  • if the receiver’s dtype is not floating-point

  • if median is non-finite, or sigma is non-finite or <= 0

Gradient¶

Not differentiable.

Examples¶

Example 1. Default median = 0, sigma = 1. Seeded, so fixed — note the one large tail value.

pluss::rng_seed(42);
auto x = pluss::series::empty({10}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
x.cauchy_();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x);

Output¶

Series(shape=[10], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=10, contiguous=true)
data=[1.8709, -2.6941, -0.9804, -1.2163, 0.0607, 0.2488, 0.8665, 1.1244, 9.4348, -1.1772]

Most values sit within a few units of 0; 9.4348 is the heavy tail showing up in a sample of just ten.

Example 2. median and sigma. Over a large sample the mean does not converge to the location, but the median does.

pluss::rng_seed(7);
auto x = pluss::series::empty({200000}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
x.cauchy_(2.0, 0.5);
std::cout << "sample mean~"   << x.mean().host<double>()[0]
          << "  sample median~" << x.median().host<double>()[0]
          << "  (location = 2)\n";

Output¶

sample mean~1.90777  sample median~2.00098  (location = 2)

With 200,000 samples the mean is still off by ~0.09 and will keep wandering; the median has pinned the location to three digits.

Example 3. Non-floating receiver, sigma <= 0, and non-finite parameters are rejected.

try {
  auto i = pluss::series::empty({3}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
  i.cauchy_();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string m = e.what();
  std::cout << m.substr(0, m.find('\n')) << "\n";
}
try {
  auto f = pluss::series::empty({3}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  f.cauchy_(0.0, 0.0);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string m = e.what();
  std::cout << m.substr(0, m.find('\n')) << "\n";
}
try {
  auto f = pluss::series::empty({3}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  f.cauchy_(std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity(), 1.0);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string m = e.what();
  std::cout << m.substr(0, m.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

cauchy_: receiver must have a floating-point dtype
cauchy_: expected finite parameters with sigma > 0
cauchy_: expected finite parameters with sigma > 0

Example 4. Reproducible under a fixed seed.

pluss::rng_seed(5);
auto a = pluss::series::empty({6}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64); a.cauchy_(0.0, 2.0);
pluss::rng_seed(5);
auto b = pluss::series::empty({6}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64); b.cauchy_(0.0, 2.0);
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "a == b: " << a.equal(b) << "\n";

Output¶

a == b: true

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • No finite mean or variance. Never summarize Cauchy samples with mean / std — use median and quantile. Do not feed them into code that assumes a finite variance.

  • Samples are unbounded in both directions and large excursions are far more common than under a normal law. A downstream clamp or robust loss may be needed.

  • Floating-point receiver only; sigma must be strictly positive.

  • Reproducible only after pluss::rng_seed(seed); each call advances the stream.

  • Not differentiable.

Summary¶

cauchy_(median = 0, sigma = 1) fills the receiver in place with heavy-tailed Cauchy samples:

  • symmetric about median; sigma sets the half-width

  • no finite mean or variance — summarize with the median, not the mean

  • built by inverse-CDF (tan) from a uniform draw; floating-point receiver only

  • reproducible under pluss::rng_seed(seed); not differentiable; aliases see the write

See Also¶

  • Series::normal_: the finite-variance location-scale sampler — reach for this unless you specifically want heavy tails.

  • Series::log_normal_: heavy right tail, but positive and with finite moments.

  • Series::uniform_: the uniform fill cauchy_ transforms internally.
